item.title: Google Integrates Model Context Protocol to Support Third-Party AI Agents in Google Home
item.description:
Google Integrates Model Context Protocol to Support Third-Party AI Agents in Google Home

Google is opening its smart home ecosystem to third-party AI agents, allowing tools such as Claude, Hermes, and Open Claw to access and control connected devices. This integration utilizes the standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP) to enable these agents to analyze home data and monitor the Google Home ecosystem on behalf of the user.

🧩 How it works

The integration connects a user’s chosen AI agent to real-world events and device history within the home. Taylor Lehman, group product manager at Google Home & Nest, stated in a blog post that the system “allows any AI agents that support MCP, including Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes or Open Claw, to securely work with all of the devices and event history in your Google Home ecosystem.”

  • Data Access: Agents have access to the underlying data and control layer of the home.
  • Third-Party Interfaces: MCP adds a layer of control where agents interact with devices through their own interfaces rather than strictly through Google-native apps.
  • Technical Requirements: Setup requires the creation of a Google Cloud project configured to use the Home MCP.

⚙️ Key details

The Home MCP integration enables several new capabilities for smart home management and monitoring:

  • Analysis: Agents can perform cross-camera analysis, such as identifying when a child arrived home from school, or review device state history to calculate utility usage or laundry cycles.
  • Voice Interaction: Agents can send audio messages over Google Home speakers to notify users when tasks are finished.
  • Customization: Users can have their agents build custom dashboards to control their Google Home devices.
  • Safety Protections: Google enforces rate limits and safety restrictions; for instance, agents are not permitted to unlock doors.
Agent or Tool Description
Claude A third-party AI agent with access to the home data and control layer.
Open Claw An AI tool capable of accessing and controlling connected devices via MCP.
Google Antigravity An agentic coding tool used to build custom AI agents for the smart home.
Gemini for Home Google’s primary interface for interacting with Google Home via the Home app and Nest speakers.

💡 Why it matters

While Google recently transitioned Gemini for Home into a full-stack AI offering, this MCP integration allows for a more open ecosystem. However, Taylor Lehman noted that “connecting it to Home MCP can result in unexpected or even undesired behavior,” recommending that users review developer policies. Developers must also consider Google’s history with discontinued smart home platforms, such as Android @ Home, Weave, and Works with Nest, when deciding to build for this new integration.

🚀 Availability

At launch, access is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced users in the United States. The service costs $20 per month or $200 per year, with access expected to roll out in the coming weeks.

item.title: Google Home integrates Model Context Protocol for third-party AI agents
item.description:
Google Home integrates Model Context Protocol for third-party AI agents

Google is opening its smart home ecosystem to third-party AI agents through the standardized Model Context Protocol (MCP). This integration allows external agents to access and control connected devices and analyze home data.

🔍 Overview

Home MCP integration connects chosen AI agents to real-world events, allowing them to act on a user’s behalf. This adds a layer of control that lets third-party agents interact directly with Google Home devices through their own interfaces. This does not replace Gemini for Home, which remains Google’s interface for the Home app and Google Nest smart speakers.

🧩 How it works

According to Taylor Lehman, group product manager at Google Home & Nest, the integration “allows any AI agents that support MCP, including Google Antigravity, Claude, Hermes or Open Claw, to securely work with all of the devices and event history in your Google Home ecosystem.”

Capabilities include:

  • Data Analysis: Using device state history to determine how many loads of laundry were done in a week or how long lights remained on.
  • Cross-Camera Analysis: Asking an agent what a child did when arriving home from school.
  • Direct Interaction: Agents can send audio messages over Google Home speakers upon completing a task.
  • Customization: Agents can create custom dashboards to control the Google Home.

⚙️ Key details

Feature Description
Security Enforces rate limits and safety protections, such as preventing agents from unlocking doors
Setup Requires creating and configuring a Google Cloud project to use Home MCP
Developer Tools Google provides the Antigravity coding tool to build custom AI agents

🚀 Availability

At launch, availability is limited to Google Home Premium Advanced users in the US, costing $20 per month or $200 per year. Access is rolling out in the coming weeks.

item.title: Ugreen launches HomeAgent: local AI hub for smart homes
item.description:
Ugreen launches HomeAgent: local AI hub for smart homes

Ugreen, known for its phone power banks, chargers, and NAS storage solutions, is moving into the smart home — in a big way.

🔍 Overview

  • This week at the IFA tech show, the company launched its HomeAgent smart home platform that combines security camera storage, on-device AI, and smart home control in one system, managed by a voice assistant called Uliya, with the promise that everything runs locally.
  • Ugreen’s HomeAgent combines a NAS, a security camera NVR, and an on-device AI assistant in one box, maxing out with a $9,999 Nvidia Jetson Thor version.

🧩 How it works

  • At the core of Ugreen’s HomeAgent system is a hub that acts as the brain of your smart home, running a local-first AI (with some caveats) that you can interact with using natural language via Uliya.
  • There are three hub configurations to choose from, each of which stores all data locally and processes video footage on-device, keeping it local and private and without monthly subscription fees.
  • Ugreen says its powerful AI runs on the hub, providing features like cross-camera tracking, smart alerts for people, vehicles, pets, and packages, and live status questions such as “where is my pet now?”.
  • There’s also AI-powered video search and text descriptions of events, along with natural language voice control of smart home devices and automations.
  • While everything can run locally on the HomeAgent, features such as push notifications and remote viewing of your security camera footage require internet access.
  • There is also an option to use the cloud for the Uliya voice assistant.

⚙️ Key details

  • Along with local storage of your camera footage, the system can store personal files, including music, movies, and photos, just like a NAS.
  • All this comes without monthly storage fees for video footage that are common with popular cloud‑based solutions, such as Amazon’s Ring and Alexa and Google’s Nest cameras and Gemini for Home.

Model lineup

Model Price Compute
HA100 $899 basic hub
HA100 Pro $2,999 adds semantic and context‑aware understanding
MasterAgent MA100 $9,999 NVIDIA Jetson Thor T5000 platform

📦 Compatibility & ecosystem

  • Both systems use the Matter smart home standard to incorporate smart home devices from different brands.
  • The HomeAgent hub is a Matter controller and will support third‑party devices using Wi‑Fi, Zigbee, Thread, Bluetooth, NFC, ONVIF/RTSP, and PoE.
  • Ugreen says it will publish a device compatibility list, which is currently fairly small and includes devices from Aqara, ThirdReality, SwitchBot, and Eve.
  • In theory, any Matter device should work, but the first phase supports only lights, switches, sensors, and curtains — and the company advises sticking with products it has approved.
  • I visited Ugreen’s booth at IFA and got a hands‑on demo, where I controlled Nanoleaf lights alongside smart blinds with voice commands to Uliya via the HomeAgent hub.
  • Ugreen is also launching a smart speaker to run Uliya, along with a line of security cameras: the SynCare Indoor Cam ID500 Pro, the SynCare POE Cam OD600 Pro, and a battery‑powered SynCare Cam OD800 Pro.
  • A unique integration is with Ugreen’s new E Ink Spectra‑powered digital photo frame that can display your photos stored on the hub, which again need never go into the cloud.

🚀 Availability

  • The HomeAgent HA100 will launch with early bird pricing of $899 which increases to $2999 of the HA100 Pro, and a whopping $9999 for the Nvidia‑powered MasterAgent MA100 model.
  • The systems will launch on Kickstarter in October, after which Ugreen suggests that pricing will roughly double.
  • Companies like SwitchBot, Reolink, and Aqara have made moves in this space, and this week at IFA, Anker launched a similar product called the Eufy MindBase.

💡 Why it matters

  • The big pitch is that your data never needs to leave your home, addressing two key smart‑home concerns: privacy and recurring subscriptions.
  • Keeping all your data inside your home, while still enjoying the benefits AI can bring to managing your smart home and digital life, is a compelling idea.
  • Whether Ugreen’s Home Agent succeeds will depend on how well it integrates with what you already own and how easy it is to set up and use.

#Ugreen #SmartHome #LocalAI #Privacy

Source: This NAS company wants to run your local smart home
